bio.en: Matt LeMay is a longtime product leader and author of Product Management in Practice, a practical guide used by hundreds of product teams.
bio.zh: 马特·勒梅（Matt LeMay）是一位资深产品负责人，也是实用指南《Product Management in Practice》的作者，该书被数百个产品团队使用。

summary.en: Matt warns that too many teams are "doing work around the work," a dynamic he calls the low-impact PM death spiral. He urges PMs to ask whether they'd fully fund their own team if they were CEO. The episode offers a three-step path toward becoming a higher-impact product team focused on outcomes.
summary.zh: 马特警示，太多团队在"围绕工作做工作"，他把这种状态称为"低影响力 PM 的死亡螺旋"。他敦促 PM 自问：如果自己是 CEO，是否会全额资助自己的团队？本期提供了一条三步路径，帮助团队转向聚焦成果、更高影响力的产品运作。

turns.speaker: Matt LeMay
turns.en: More product managers and teams are getting laid off. The problem is the message that Daniel Ek from Spotify sent out with their layoffs in 2024, we still have too many teams doing work around the work.
turns.zh: 越来越多的产品经理和团队面临裁员。问题在于Spotify的丹尼尔·埃克在2024年裁员时传递出的信息——我们仍有太多团队在围绕工作而工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Even if you are told to build the thing that the execs are really excited about, you're still going to get fired eventually.
turns.zh: 即便被要求去开发高管们真正兴奋不已的项目，最终你还是会被裁掉。

turns.speaker: Matt LeMay
turns.en: If you were the CEO of this company, would you fully fund your own team? Frankly, most of the people I ask that question to don't know the answer right away.
turns.zh: 如果你身为这家公司的CEO，你会全力资助自己的团队吗？坦白说，我问过这个问题的大多数人一时都答不上来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Which is something you call the low impact PM Death Spiral.
turns.zh: 这就是所谓的“低影响力产品经理死亡螺旋”。

turns.speaker: Matt LeMay
turns.en: Is the dynamic in which every medium to large company I've ever worked with finds itself in, one way or another. (00:00:33): It starts with adding little features here and there, making little cosmetic improvements until the next round of layoffs.
turns.zh: 这是我曾工作过的每一家中大型公司都深陷其中的怪圈。（00:00:33）：先是零星添加一些小功能，进行表面上的改进，直到下一轮裁员。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You have three steps to become more of an impact first product team.
turns.zh: 要成为更有影响力的首席产品团队，你需要分三步。

turns.speaker: Matt LeMay
turns.en: So the first is in setting team goals, no more than one step away from company goals. Don't let it get cascaded into oblivion.
turns.zh: 第一步是设定团队目标，确保与公司目标紧密相连。切忌让目标逐渐被淡忘。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You're an ICPM. It's up to you. No excuses.
turns.zh: 你是一名ICPM（独立贡献产品经理）。全靠你自己，没有借口。

turns.speaker: Matt LeMay
turns.en: You can follow all the best practices, but if your company goes out of business, they're not going to keep writing your paycheck for two years because all of your OKRs were a 0. 6 or a 0.7.
turns.zh: 你可以遵循所有最佳实践，但如果公司倒闭了，他们不会因为你的OKR（目标与关键结果）得分是0分或0.7分，就继续给你发两年工资。

提升你的职业生涯，本次峰会将为你带来实用的洞见，助力你的团队更进一步。（00:04:12）：注册通道已开放，但名额有限。请前往pragmaticinstitute.com /Lenny（注意网址中的“/Lenny”）立即锁定席位。（00:04:26）：马特，非常感谢你能做客我们的播客，欢迎加入我们。

turns.speaker: Matt LeMay
turns.en: Thank you so much for having me. I'm really, really excited to be here.
turns.zh: 非常感谢您邀请我。我真的非常兴奋能来到这里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm even more excited. You have a really interesting background. I usually don't spend time on background, but I thought this would be fun. (00:04:38): I was looking at your LinkedIn and your background. The beginning of your career you spent 13 years at Pitchfork reviewing music.
turns.zh: 我甚至更兴奋了。您的背景非常有趣。我通常不会花时间谈论背景，但我觉得这次会很有趣。（00:04:38）我查看了您的领英资料和背景。您职业生涯的开端是在Pitchfork工作了13年，负责音乐评论。

turns.speaker: Matt LeMay
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Reviewing artists. Pitchfork was a massive deal. I don't know where it is today, but it was the most influential music review site. Is it still a big deal or is it less so?
turns.zh: 评论艺术家。Pitchfork曾是家喻户晓的品牌。我不知道它如今的处境如何，但它曾是最具影响力的音乐评论网站。它现在还是重要平台吗？还是没那么受关注了？

turns.speaker: Matt LeMay
turns.en: It is still a big deal. It was much less of a big deal when I started working for them and I was a 16-year-old music nerd, writing record reviews in my bedroom at my parents' apartment.
turns.zh: 它依然很重要。我刚开始在那里工作时，还是个16岁的音乐迷，在父母家里的卧室里写唱片评论。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so what I'm hearing is you helped make them a big deal. Excellent. That's impacts. We're going to talk all about impact.
turns.zh: 好的，看来您为它的发展做出了贡献。太棒了。这就是影响力所在。我们接下来要深入探讨影响力的话题。

turns.speaker: Matt LeMay
turns.en: If I were better at telling my own story, that's exactly what I'd be saying, is that before I started, I was product manager number one at Pitchfork.
turns.zh: 如果我更善于讲述自己的故事，我肯定会说，加入Pitchfork之前，我曾是那里首位产品经理。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Funny enough, you look at your resume, you went into product management from Pitchfork. Very typical career path. (00:05:23): By the way, if you're on YouTube watching, there's a lot of musical paraphernalia behind you, an awesome guitar, so clearly there's a thread of music throughout your background.
turns.zh: 说真的，看看您的简历，从Pitchfork转行做产品经理，真是典型的职业发展路径。（00:05:23）顺便说一句，如果您在YouTube上观看视频，您身后有很多音乐周边物品，一把很棒的吉他，看来音乐始终贯穿您的职业生涯。

turns.speaker: Matt LeMay
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let me ask you this question: what is most similar about making music, and even critiquing music, and building great product?
turns.zh: 我想问您一个问题：在音乐创作、音乐评论和产品开发之间，最相似的方面是什么？

turns.speaker: Matt LeMay
turns.en: The magic lies in the way people work together. That's really what I think has been the consistent thread between all the work that I've done. (00:05:47): I spent years as a touring musician. I still occasionally tour in my friend Will Chef's band. And it's that magic of people with different perspectives, different ideas, building into something that is somehow greater than the sum of its individual parts and perspectives. (00:06:03): That's what makes this interesting. That's what makes music magical. That's what makes product development interesting, especially in the age of AI. (00:06:13): When people have the opportunity to, I think, close themselves off from the messier parts of human interaction, from those moments where you realize that your perspective might be limited, that somebody else might be able to expose you to something, show you a way of working, show you a way of seeing that you haven't seen before, I think that those interactions, that ability to learn from and build with each other, is only going to become more valuable and more precious, frankly, as technology continues to do what technology does.
turns.zh: 关键在于团队协作的魔力。这是我认为自己所做的一切工作的共同主线（00:05:47）。我曾作为巡演音乐人多年，现在偶尔还会在朋友Will Chef的乐队中演出。正是不同视角、不同想法的人共同创造出比各部分之和更伟大的成果的魔力（00:06:03）。这就是其趣味所在。这也是音乐的魔力所在。这也是产品开发的魅力所在，尤其是在人工智能时代（00:06:13）。当人们有机会将自己封闭在人类互动的混乱之外，远离那些让你意识到自己视野有限的时刻，远离那些能让你接触到新观点、展示新工作方式、呈现新视角的时刻时，我认为这种互动、相互学习和共同创造的能力只会变得越来越宝贵和珍贵，坦白说，随着技术不断发挥其作用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, what a beautiful answer.
turns.zh: 哇，多么精彩的回答。

turns.speaker: Matt LeMay
turns.en: Thank you.
turns.zh: 谢谢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. So let's get to the task at hand.
turns.zh: 我太喜欢了。那么，让我们开始今天的任务吧。

turns.speaker: Matt LeMay
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So you're known for writing one of the most popular books in the field of product management called Product Management in Practice.
turns.zh: 您因撰写了产品管理领域最受欢迎的书籍之一《Product Management in Practice》而闻名。

turns.speaker: Matt LeMay
turns.en: I suppose I am.
turns.zh: 我想我确实是。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yes. Basically describes the job of a product manager very practically, very specifically, better than any other book out there. (00:07:09): You have a new book out called Impact First Product Teams. I asked you what the goal of this book was and you said the goal was what are the steps that individual product teams can take to align their work to business critical outcomes, regardless of how their organizations approach product development? (00:07:25): And I thought this was a really nice way of framing this conversation. There's two important parts to the sentence that you gave me. (00:07:32): One is aligning your work to business critical outcomes, and the other is steps an individual product team can take, regardless of other business functions. (00:07:40): So let me start with this first part. This is kind of you named your book after this concept of impact, first: Why is aligning work to impact and to business critical outcomes so important?
turns.zh: 是的。这本书实际上非常务实、非常具体地描述了产品经理的工作，比市面上其他任何书籍都做得更好。（00:07:09）：你新出版了一本书，名为《以影响力为先的产品团队》。我问你这本书的目标是什么，你说目标是，无论组织如何开展产品开发工作，各个产品团队都可以采取哪些步骤来使他们的工作与对业务至关重要的成果保持一致？（00:07:25）：我认为这是一种非常好的谈话框架。你给我的句子中有两个重要部分。（00:07:32）：一是使工作与对业务至关重要的成果保持一致，二是各个产品团队可以采取的步骤，而不受其他业务职能的限制。（00:07:40）：所以让我先从第一部分开始。这本书以"影响力优先"这个概念命名：为什么使工作与影响力和对业务至关重要的成果保持一致如此重要？

turns.speaker: Matt LeMay
turns.en: It's important because at the end of the day, it is those business critical outcomes against which you and your team will be evaluated. That's the reality of working for a business, right? (00:08:02): If you are contributing to the business in a way that the business at large can understand, that the CEO can understand, that the CFO can understand, if your team is a good investment for the business, then the business will continue making that investment. (00:08:16): If your team is not a good investment for the business or you don't really know if your team is a good investment for the business, but you figure you're showing up, so probably it's fine, you guess, then that puts you in a really tenuous position, and a position that I think we've all seen not work out terribly well for everybody in recent history.
turns.zh: 这很重要，因为归根结底，正是这些对业务至关重要的成果将成为衡量你和你的团队的标准。这就是为企业工作的现实，对吧？（00:08:02）：如果你以一种整个企业都能理解的方式为企业做出贡献——CEO能理解，CFO能理解——如果你的团队对企业来说是一项好的投资，那么企业会继续进行这项投资。（00:08:16）：如果你的团队对企业来说不是一项好的投资，或者你不确定你的团队是否是一项好的投资，但你觉得自己在努力工作，可能就没问题，那么这会让你处于一个非常不稳定的境地，我认为我们最近都见过很多人因为这种情况而遭遇不好的结果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so, what is this a reaction to? Because I imagine many people hearing this are, like, "Of course, PMs, product teams we're driving business impact, well, that's why we're here." (00:08:44): That's not actually the case in most cases. So first of all, just what is this reaction to? Is this the reaction to people being, like, "Oh, we're just going to build great products, we're going to listen to customers,"? Talk about the flip side of this.
turns.zh: 那么，这是对什么的反应呢？因为我想很多听到这话的人会说，"当然，产品经理、产品团队，我们要推动业务影响力，这就是我们存在的意义。"（00:08:44）：但在大多数情况下并非如此。所以首先，这是一种什么样的反应？是针对那些说"哦，我们只需要打造优秀的产品，倾听客户需求"的人吗？谈谈这背后的另一面。

turns.speaker: Matt LeMay
turns.en: I mean, there's a couple of things. I think the main one is just more product managers and teams are getting laid off. That's a really scary reality right now. (00:09:05): And if you look at the messages that are being conveyed by CEOs when they lay off these teams, some of them are pretty clear. (00:09:13): The message that Daniel Ek from Spotify sent out with their layoffs in 2024 said, "We still have too many teams doing work around the work and supporting work, rather than focusing on opportunities with real impact." (00:09:25): And that really struck a nerve because I've been on those supporting teams before. I've done the work around the work. And I've assumed that if I was given work around the work to do, that surely it must be critical to the business, otherwise they wouldn't have hired me to do it. (00:09:40): I don't think that is a safe assumption to make. I think especially given that we are no longer in a zero interest rate environment, given that hiring and retaining employees is expensive, given that companies are looking at cost savings, I think we are in a moment where it is really incumbent upon each product team and each member of each product team to be able to understand, articulate, and work towards the top line business impact of their own work.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，有几个方面。其中最主要的是越来越多的产品经理和团队被裁员。这确实是当下令人担忧的现实。（00:09:05）：如果你看看CEO们在裁员时传递的信息，有些话说得很清楚。（00:09:13）：Spotify的丹尼尔·埃克在2024年裁员时发出的信息是：“我们仍然有太多团队在围绕工作做工作，支持工作，而不是专注于有真正影响力的机会。” （00:09:25）：这真的触动了我的神经，因为我以前也曾在那些支持性团队中工作过。我也做过围绕工作的工作。我曾以为，如果我被安排做围绕工作的工作，肯定对业务至关重要，否则他们不会雇我来做这些工作。（00:09:40）：我认为这种假设并不安全。特别是考虑到我们不再处于零利率环境，招聘和留住员工成本高昂，公司正在寻求成本节约，我认为我们正处于一个关键时刻，每个产品团队和每个团队成员都必须能够理解、清晰表达并致力于实现自身工作的商业影响力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. So where this comes from is, one, if you are not driving something that is directly driving business growth, you're not as valuable to the company. You're the kind of person that they'd lay off.
turns.zh: 太棒了。那么这种情况的根源在于，如果你没有直接推动业务增长，你对公司就没有价值了。你就是那种会被裁掉的人。

turns.speaker: Matt LeMay
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's also a flip side of finding a job. It feels like if you have shown impact in your resume, "Here's all the impact I've driven," this also helps you get hired. True?
turns.zh: 找工作的另一面是，如果你在简历中展示了影响力，“看，我推动了这些影响力”，这也能帮助你获得工作。对吧？

turns.speaker: Matt LeMay
turns.en: Absolutely. Yeah. I mean, it's the most common resume advice I see, is show the number, show the impact, say what you did. (00:10:40): I have a friend who does resume coaching, and I showed her my resume a couple of years ago. And she said, "I love your resume except for one thing. Why do you write like a little girl? Say what you did, say what your contributions were. Don't say 'I helped. I may have maybe helped people do this'. Say the impact. Put the number on it." And I think I needed to hear that from her because I think there is a tendency, especially for those of us who do really thrive in that collaborative environment, who our nature is to not want to take credit for work that could only exist via the contributions of many people with diverse experiences and perspectives. (00:11:22): It's really hard to say, "Well, I did this and I contributed to that," but that's part of why I wrote this book at the team level, because I think for folks, like myself, who really enjoy and thrive in that team environment, if you can look at the product team as the foundational unit of impact and say, "We delivered this. We were able to work together to have this impact for the business," that feels really good and also speaks directly to the work that that team did together.
turns.zh: 绝对的。是的。我的意思是，我看到最常见的简历建议就是，展示数字，展示影响力，说你做了什么。（00:10:40）：我有个做简历指导的朋友，几年前我给她看了我的简历。她说：“除了一个地方，我都喜欢你的简历。为什么你写得像个小女孩？说你做了什么，说你的贡献是什么。别说‘我帮过忙。可能帮过别人做这件事’。说出影响力。把数字写上。” 我觉得我需要听她这么说。因为我觉得我们这些在协作环境中茁壮成长的人，有一种倾向，就是不想把功劳归于自己，因为很多工作只有在众多具有不同经验和观点的人的贡献下才能实现。（00:11:22）：很难说“嗯，我做了这个，我为那个做出了贡献”，但这正是我在团队层面写这本书的部分原因，因为我认为像我这样真正喜欢并在团队环境中茁壮成长的人，如果你能把产品团队视为产生影响力的基础单位，并说：“我们实现了这个目标。我们能够一起为业务创造这种影响力。”这感觉很棒，也直接说明了团队共同完成的工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a really interesting insight. I think a lot of this comes from just PMs naturally are trained to deflect credit and to include, say 'we' in everything and just this person did that. So I get where that comes from. So most listeners will probably still be thinking, "Yes, I'm driving impact, I'm great. I don't have a problem here. I don't to change, need to change anything." What are some ways to stress test your thinking? Maybe some questions to ask yourself or maybe your team of just, like, "Okay, maybe I'm not?"
turns.zh: 这真是个很有意思的见解。我认为很多产品经理天生就被训练得善于推卸功劳，比如在汇报时总爱说“我们”如何如何，而把功劳归于某个具体人员。所以我能理解这种心理。然而大多数听众可能还是会想：“没错，我确实在推动项目进展，我很棒。我这儿没问题，不需要改变现状。”那怎样才能检验自己的思维呢？或许可以问问自己，或者让团队成员思考：“好吧，也许我做得不够好？”

turns.speaker: Matt LeMay
turns.en: So the first question I ask most of the teams I work with is if you were the CEO of this company, would you fully fund your own team? (00:12:29): And that is a small question that can provoke some big reactions. Because, for me, when I was working as a product manager, I truly believed that my job was to find the next most defensible thing to build, build it, celebrate it, find the next most defensible thing to build, and so on and so forth. Rinse and repeat forever and ever. (00:12:53): I kind of assumed that the existence of my team was this righteous fact of the universe, right? My team would always be there for all time, and it was just a matter of us finding the next thing to work on, which meant doing discovery and making concessions to what leadership wanted and doing all that stakeholder management. (00:13:13): But the idea that my team came at a cost to the business, that at some point somebody might look at my team on a spreadsheet and say, "Who are these very expensive people? Why do we need them? Do we actually need them?" It just wasn't something that crossed my mind because I wasn't in the room for those conversations. That wasn't how I was thinking about my team's work. (00:13:34): So I like asking this question because it's a perspective shift. It gets you thinking if you were personally accountable for the existential market-level success of this business, would you invest in your team? (00:13:52): And frankly, most of the people I ask that question to don't know the answer right away. They're not sure. They say, "I think so," or, "Yeah, yeah. Yeah, because... " And then you can see the gears turning. (00:14:05): And again, to me that is a risky situation to be in because if you can't answer that question as a member of the team, nobody else in the organization is going to be as well-equipped to answer that question as you are. (00:14:19): So bringing that question to the team, asking it and answering it proactively and collaboratively and being ready to say, "Okay, if we can't answer this confidently, what are the changes we need to make? Do we need to change our purview? Do we need to change our goals? Who do we need to talk to? What do we need to do in order to make this happen, in order to answer that question confidently?" We are much better off having that conversation at the team level than waiting for someone else to have it for us, or at us.
turns.zh: 所以我给大多数合作团队提出的第一个问题是，如果你是这家公司的CEO，你会全力资助自己的团队吗？（00:12:29）这个看似简单的问题，却能引发深刻反思。因为我自己当产品经理时，深信我的职责就是找到下一个最具商业价值的项目，推进开发，庆祝成功，再找下一个类似项目，如此循环往复。（00:12:53）我曾理所当然地认为团队的存在是宇宙的既定法则——只要不断寻找下一个可开发的方向，就能应对各种挑战，这意味着要进行市场调研、向领导妥协、处理各方利益诉求。（00:13:13）但从未想过团队的存在会给公司带来成本——当有人在财务表格上质疑“这些高昂的团队开支为何存在？我们真的需要他们吗？”这种担忧从未在我的脑海中浮现，因为我从未参与过这样的讨论。这根本不是我思考团队工作的视角。（00:13:34）所以我喜欢提这个问题，因为它能引发思维转变。它迫使你反思：如果你要为公司的市场成功亲自担责，你会投资自己的团队吗？（00:13:52）坦白说，我问过的大多数人一时答不上来。他们犹豫不决，说：“我觉得应该吧。”或者“是啊，是啊，因为……” 然后你能看到他们的大脑飞速运转。（00:14:05）对我来说，这是一个危险的局面——如果团队成员都答不上来这个问题，那么组织里其他人也同样无法胜任这项任务。（00:14:19）因此，把这个问题带入团队，主动且协作地探讨答案，并准备好说：“好吧，如果我们无法自信地回答这个问题，那我们需要做出哪些改变？是调整我们的职责范围？还是重新设定目标？需要和谁沟通？需要采取哪些行动才能自信地回答这个问题？” 在团队层面进行这样的对话，总比等待别人来替我们做要好得多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So is kind of the signal here is if you can't confidently say yes, asking yourself this question or your team talking through this and having a clear answer, there's maybe a potential problem that you need to work on?
turns.zh: 所以关键信号在于，如果你无法自信地回答“是”，或者你的团队无法通过深入讨论给出明确答案，那可能存在需要改进的地方。

turns.speaker: Matt LeMay
turns.en: Absolutely. I think that's exactly it, yeah.
turns.zh: 绝对是这样的。我觉得就是这个道理，是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And we'll talk about what to actually do and the steps you recommend to fix this problem, but I want to keep talking about impact because sometimes it takes a while for people to be convinced, "Okay, I need to really do this," versus, "Okay, here's the ways to do this."
turns.zh: 接下来我们会探讨具体该怎么做，以及你推荐的解决这个问题的步骤，但我想先继续谈谈影响力的问题，因为有时候人们需要一段时间才能被说服：“好吧，我真的得这么做了，”而不是“好吧，这里有一些做事的方法。”

turns.speaker: Matt LeMay
turns.en: Yeah. It has taken me until now, until writing this book to be convinced, and I still feel like I need to be convinced a little bit sometimes.
turns.zh: 是啊。我直到现在，直到写这本书时，才被说服，而有时我仍然觉得自己偶尔还需要被说服一下。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think the layoffs are a really good convincing function for people.
turns.zh: 我认为裁员对人们来说是一个非常有效的说服手段。

turns.speaker: Matt LeMay
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Where they're seeing all these PMs being laid off and just, like, "How do I avoid that?" And this is basically the answer to that, is here's how you avoid getting laid off. (00:15:33): There's an interesting implication in what you describe here where you encourage the PM and the product team to think like the CEO. (00:15:39): This touches on something I've been meaning to write about, but I haven't, which is a lot of people, there's this argument are PMs the mini CEO? (00:15:46): In my mind, the PM is 100% the mini CEO, in terms of they think like the CE or they should within the team. They're the same; their job is to think about the business like a CEO within the team. (00:16:03): Obviously they're not in charge of everyone. They can't let get anyone go. The reporting lines are not the same. But I feel like that's a really good lens for the job of a PM, is just you're like the mini CEO on a team, making sure you're building the right things, thinking about the business, solving real problems that matter.
turns.zh: 当他们看到那么多产品经理被裁掉时，就会想：“我该怎么避免这种情况？” 而这基本上就是答案，即这里教你如何避免被裁掉。（00:15:33）：你所描述的内容中有一些有趣的含义，你鼓励产品经理和产品团队像CEO一样思考。（00:15:39）：这触及到我一直想写但还没写的一个话题，那就是很多人都在争论产品经理是否是迷你CEO？（00:15:46）：在我看来，产品经理绝对是迷你CEO，从他们思考方式来看，他们应该在团队中像CEO一样思考。他们本质上是一样的，他们的工作就是像CEO一样思考业务。（00:16:03）：显然，他们不负责所有人。他们不能解雇任何人。汇报路线不一样。但我觉得这对产品经理的工作来说是一个很好的视角，就是你就像团队中的迷你CEO，确保你在做正确的事情，思考业务，解决真正重要的问题。

turns.speaker: Matt LeMay
turns.en: I think the way I've come to think about it is that the product manager is responsible for the whole team thinking like a CEO, if that makes sense.
turns.zh: 我认为我现在对此的理解是，产品经理有责任让整个团队像CEO一样思考，如果这能说得通的话。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个观点。

turns.speaker: Matt LeMay
turns.en: So if the product manager takes that on as their sole responsibility and says, "I'm the mini CEO. I think about the business," that's a missed opportunity. (00:16:35): In my consulting work, it's more often than not been an engineer who's actually able to get to that specific impact-level goal for the team, sometimes before the product manager does, because the engineer is thinking in systems, is thinking about, "Okay, I know this system, I know this other system. I've had this conversation with this person. I think I see how this can all fit together." (00:16:55): Sometimes it's a designer or a UX researcher who understands what customers need and who has that direct firsthand knowledge. (00:17:02): So I think the way that I certainly initially misinterpreted the mini CEO thing was you are solely in charge of this, as opposed to you are the person who brings that kind of CEO-level commercial thinking to the team. And I've been much more inclined of late to see the product manager's job as to bring in and facilitate that conversation, rather than to be the sole owner of that conversation.
turns.zh: 所以，如果产品经理把这作为自己的唯一责任，并说：“我是迷你CEO。我思考业务，”那就是错失了一个机会。（00:16:35）：在我的咨询工作中，往往是工程师能够真正为团队实现特定的影响力目标，有时甚至比产品经理更早，因为工程师在思考系统，思考：“好吧，我了解这个系统，我了解另一个系统。我和这个人讨论过。我觉得我能看清这些如何整合在一起。” （00:16:55）：有时是设计师或用户体验研究员，他们理解客户需求，拥有第一手的直接知识。（00:17:02）：所以我认为我最初对迷你CEO概念的误解是，你是唯一负责这件事的人，而不是你把这种CEO级别的商业思维带入团队的人。我最近越来越倾向于将产品经理的工作视为引入并促进这种对话，而不是独自主导这种对话。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is a really good Nuance to what I said, and it makes all the sense in the world. (00:17:34): Following these lines of what is the job for product manager, you have a really nice way of just thinking about it. What does a business expect from a product manager?
turns.zh: 这对我的说法来说确实是一个很好的补充，完全说得通。（00:17:34）：沿着产品经理的工作职责这条线，你有一种很好的思考方式。企业对产品经理有什么期望？

turns.speaker: Matt LeMay
turns.en: Yeah. My favorite definition of product management comes from Melissa Perry's book Escaping the Build Trap, where she describes product management as facilitating a value exchange.You're facilitating a value exchange between a business and its customers. (00:17:57): The actual shape and nature of that value exchange depends on so many things. It depends on your funding model, it depends on your business model, it depends on whether you're B2B or B2C, it depends on whether you're publicly traded or privately held. There are so many different variables that go into what a business expects from product teams. (00:18:19): And one thing I've come to is that I'm probably too hesitant to generalize in general, aside from that generalization I just made, but I think that the best product managers and teams I've worked with are really curious to understand what success means to their particular business. (00:18:38): So if that's a startup, how much runway do we have? What do we need to raise that next round? Are our investors looking for growth? Are they looking for profitability? What are they looking for in order for us to reach that next existential milestone? (00:18:52): If we're a publicly traded company, what are investors looking for? What have we told shareholders? What's in our next prospectus? What are we saying we're going to deliver to the market at large? (00:19:01): This information usually exists somewhere, but it's really easy to get disconnected from it as we go about the day-to-day work of doing product management. (00:19:11): I've been in a lot of rooms having workshops and sessions with teams I work with, where they're pulling up the last town hall meeting to look for slides from their CEO because they're so busy, they have so many day-to-day things to deal with, that for them that town hall day is, like, "Okay, finally I can just not have to deal with people emailing me every 10 seconds." It's a chance to take a deep breath and then get back to the stuff that really matters. (00:19:38): But those top-level things, those promises that have been made to the market at large, to the board, to the shareholders, those are often a great place to start for understanding what exactly your business is looking for, so you can figure out how your team's work helps contribute to success in the terms that matter most to the business.
turns.zh: 是啊。我最喜欢的关于产品管理的定义来自梅利莎·佩里（Melissa Perry）的书《逃离构建陷阱》（Escaping the Build Trap），她将产品管理描述为促进价值交换的过程。你是在促进企业与客户之间的价值交换。（00:17:57）：这种价值交换的实际形式和性质取决于诸多因素。它取决于你的融资模式，取决于你的商业模式，取决于你是B2B还是B2C模式，取决于你的公司是上市公司还是私营企业。企业对产品团队的期望受到诸多不同变量的影响。（00:18:19）：我逐渐意识到，除了我刚刚提到的那个概括性观点外，我可能不太愿意进行笼统的概括。但我认为，我合作过的最优秀的产品经理和团队都非常渴望了解成功对他们所在企业的具体意义。（00:18:38）：所以，如果这是一家初创公司，我们还有多少筹资时间？下一轮融资需要筹集多少资金？投资者希望看到增长吗？他们追求的是盈利能力吗？要达到下一个关键里程碑，他们需要满足哪些条件？（00:18:52）：如果我们是一家上市公司，投资者关注什么？我们向股东传达了怎样的信息？下一份招股说明书里有什么内容？我们对外宣称要为市场提供怎样的产品？（00:19:01）：这些信息通常都存在于某个地方，但在日常产品管理工作中，我们很容易与之脱节。（00:19:11）：我参加过很多与合作团队的研讨会，他们会翻出上次CEO举行的全员大会的幻灯片，因为他们太忙了，日常事务太多，以至于那天开会就是为了能暂时不处理每隔十分钟就有人发邮件求助的情况。这是他们喘口气、重新专注于真正重要工作的机会。（00:19:38）：但那些高层目标，那些向市场、董事会、股东做出的承诺，往往是理解企业真正需求的绝佳切入点，这样你就能弄清楚你的团队如何能以对企业最重要的方式为成功做出贡献。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's an amazing segue to exactly where I'd wanted to go, which is this quote that is exactly what you just said, the question you should be asking, it's kind of a different version of the one you shared earlier, which is what are we doing to contribute to the success of the business?
turns.zh: 这真是完美地引出了我接下来想讨论的重点，那就是你刚刚提到的这句话——你应该问的问题。这是和你之前分享的那个问题的不同版本，那个问题是我们如何为企业的成功做出贡献？

turns.speaker: Matt LeMay
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what is it that you think people are thinking instead most often?
turns.zh: 那么你认为人们最常犯的错误思维是什么？

turns.speaker: Matt LeMay
turns.en: It's interesting. We live in a world where for the last 20 years of product development, we've been all about best practices. We love best practices. (00:20:30): And I love best practices too. I think best practices can be really valuable, can be really useful. I love how much knowledge sharing there is out there. When I started 15 years ago, it was so much harder to get any sense of how anybody was doing anything. (00:20:44): But I think the downside of this is that there are a lot of folks who are really, really fixated on doing things the right way. And a lot of the writing and thinking about doing things the right way exists in kind of this middle layer, between impact and day-to-day work. (00:21:03): So if you have impact, the overall success of the business, revenue, growth, profits. Then from there you set objectives and you do initiatives, and then you do bets, and then you make a strategy, and then you do your day-to-day work. (00:21:15): I think the tendency among a lot of product teams is to key to those middle pieces, to say, "Okay, what we're doing is on strategy. What we're doing is part of objectives. We did OKRs, right? We spent three weeks coming up with our OKRs for three months. It's OKR season, everybody. We have to pretend to care about our goals, and I read a book that says we have to have five to seven objectives with five to seven key results, and we want the score of each one to be a 0.6 or a 0.7." (00:21:41): And at the end of the day, you've actually spent so much time and energy being really clever and cascading these things into these intermediate steps, that each step has incurred more and more risk that we might not achieve that impact we seek to drive. (00:21:59): Each time we abstract things out, each time we cascade things from impact to something else until we wind up with a checklist of features to build, we're assuming that if we then build that checklist of features... We will have a successful business. (00:22:14): But honestly, most of the companies and teams I work with, if I ask them how their lowest-level goals add up to their highest-level goals, they look at me like I just asked them the most impossible question in the world. (00:22:27): Because by the time you get things down to that level, maybe it's going to work, maybe it's not going to work. There are assumptions baked into each of those levels. (00:22:37): You might go through the motions of doing OKRs the right way or doing strategy the right way, but that doesn't guarantee that your strategy is going to work. It doesn't mean that your OKRs are going to add up to what your investors or your shareholders need to see. (00:22:52): So I think there's a tendency among product teams to really sweat the middle, and to get really stressed out if the middle is not in perfect theoretical harmony with itself. If the objectives are a little out of line with the initiatives, are a little out of line with the bets, are a little out of line with the domains. (00:23:14): But at the end of the day, I don't think I've ever worked for a company where these things add up to a perfect breadcrumb trail you can trace back from, "We prioritized these bits of work in this sprint because it adds up to this objective, which is part of this strategy, which adds up to this initiative, which is part of this bet, which will deliver this much impact." It's just not how things work in the real world.
turns.zh: 真有意思。我们生活在一个过去20年产品开发都执着于最佳实践的世界里。我们热爱最佳实践。（00:20:30）我也喜欢最佳实践。我认为它们确实很有价值、非常实用。我很欣赏当下知识共享的氛围。15年前我刚入行时，想了解别人怎么做事可要困难得多了。（00:20:44）但这也带来了负面影响——太多人过于执着于"正确"的做事方式。很多关于最佳实践的思考和写作都停留在影响力与日常工作之间的灰色地带。（00:21:03）如果你的目标是业务的整体成功——营收、增长、利润——那么你会设定目标、开展行动、进行赌注，最后制定战略，再开展日常工作。（00:21:15）我发现很多产品团队容易陷入这些中间环节的细节里，比如："好吧，我们现在在做战略部分。我们的目标是OKR，对吧？我们花了三周时间制定了三个月的OKR。现在是OKR季了，大家都要假装在乎目标。我读过一本书，说要设定5到7个目标，每个目标对应5到7个关键结果，每个结果的得分要达到0.6或0.7。" （00:21:41）到头来，大家为了把这些步骤合理化，反而增加了风险，离实现预期影响力越来越远。（00:21:59）每次我们把事情抽象化、从影响力层层拆解到最终的功能清单时，都假定只要按清单开发就能成功。（00:22:14）但说实话，我合作过的大多数公司和团队，如果问他们底层目标如何与顶层目标衔接，他们都会一脸茫然。（00:22:27）因为当你把事情落实到具体层面时，可能成功也可能失败。每个层级都隐含着各种假设。（00:22:37）你可能按部就班地完成OKR或战略制定，但这并不能保证策略有效，也不意味着OKR能满足投资人或股东的需求。（00:22:52）所以产品团队容易纠结于中间环节，执着于让各个层级完美契合。但说到底，我从未在任何公司见过这些环节能形成一条完美的逻辑链条："我们在这次冲刺中优先处理这些工作，目的是达成这个目标，而这个目标是战略的一部分，最终能转化为这项行动，最终带来预期影响力。" 现实世界可不是这样运作的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like a lot of listeners are, like, "That sounds very familiar," exactly what you just described. Again, we're going to talk about what to change and how to make work better to actually align your teams with impact. But I want to first talk about something that follows this thread you're on, which is something you call the Low Impact PM Death Spiral. Talk about what that looks like.
turns.zh: 我感觉很多听众会觉得，“这听起来很耳熟”，正如你刚才描述的那样。接下来我们会探讨如何做出改变，让工作更高效，从而真正让团队与成果形成协同。但首先，我想先谈谈你提到的这个核心问题——低效能项目经理的恶性循环。请你详细讲讲这种情况是怎样的。

turns.speaker: Matt LeMay
turns.en: The Death Spiral.
turns.zh: 恶性循环。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love the hands.
turns.zh: 我喜欢你比喻的手势。

turns.speaker: Matt LeMay
turns.en: The Low Impact Death Spiral is the dynamic in which every-
turns.zh: 低效能恶性循环指的是一种动态循环，表现为每件事——

turns.speaker: Matt LeMay
turns.en: ... impact death spiral is the dynamic in which every medium to large company I've ever worked with finds itself in one way or another. And honestly, a lot of small product companies do as well, and it goes something like this. It starts with teams taking on low impact work. Adding little features here and there, making little cosmetic improvements because it's easier, it invites less scrutiny and you're less likely to mess up something important, right? The analogy I use sometimes is if you're working on a car, if you put your hands in the engine, you might make the car run really well or you might make it so that the car doesn't run at all. If you have the option of doing that or decking out the car with a paint job and rhinestones and making it look really, really cool, what are you going to choose to do? I know for me, I would choose the rhinestones every time because then the car runs however it runs. Whoever else is the expert in engines can fix the engine, but I'm going to do this thing which everyone can see. All the executives can look at it and say, "Wow, look at how cool this car looks," and it's not going to do any harm, right? What's the worst that could happen? We can always take the paint off. (00:25:15): The problem is if you have 10 teams adding rhinestones to a car, eventually the hood of the car is going to be so heavy that you can't lift it to get to the engine anymore, and that's exactly what happens in most product organizations. As you have more and more teams adding in these little features, making little enhancements, adding features, which might get some usage, but they're not going to take away anything meaningful, they're not going to mess with the commercial engine of the business. You have more folks building in and the hood of the car gets heavier and heavier, the product gets more and more complicated. (00:25:50): You have all these little bits that have little dependencies on each other and the product becomes as, I think most modern products are a collection of loosely connected features rather than a single guided experience. What does that mean? That means internally, building anything becomes a lot harder, right? Because there's 10 product teams that have to manage dependencies whenever you want to build something, so companies start adding program management layers. They're like, "We have too many meetings. We need to reorg for program management because reorgs fix everything and we need to make sure that we have all these layers and people are connected and we're doing dependency management." But as you add more of those things, it becomes harder and harder to do high-impact work. (00:26:33): The hood just gets heavier and heavier and heavier, which in turn sends teams deeper and deeper down the rabbit hole of low-impact work. Low-impact work begets low-impact work. The more low-impact work you do, the harder it is to do high-impact work, the more likely you are to do low-impact work and so on and so forth. It goes and goes and goes until the next round of layoffs, and this is a real problem. (00:27:01): I've experienced this at again, pretty much every company I've worked with, and it's been really interesting to see how often the breaking of that cycle comes down to individual product teams being brave enough to look at their own work and look at what matters to the business and say, "You know what? We are not going to incur the risk of being a low-impact team anymore. We are going to proactively seek out high- impact work and we're going to deliver, even if it means we have to coordinate with a lot of other teams. Even if it means that suddenly the executive team takes a really big interest in the work that we're doing. We're going to see that as signs that the work we're doing matters not as things that are going to be an impediment to getting the work done."
turns.zh:
……影响力螺旋式下降的现象，是我曾合作过的每一家中型到大型公司都曾陷入的死循环。说实话，很多小型产品公司也会深陷其中。整个过程大致是这样的：团队首先接手低影响力的工作。他们到处添加一些小功能，进行一些表面上的改进，因为这样既容易上手，又能避免被过度审视，降低出错的风险，对吧？我常用的一个比喻是，如果你在修车时，把手伸进引擎里，你可能会让车子运行得非常顺畅，也可能让它彻底无法启动。如果你有机会选择，是去改进引擎，还是给车子喷漆、贴水钻让它看起来超酷，你会选哪个？我知道我每次都会选水钻，因为引擎坏了总有人能修，而我做的这些改动大家都能看到。高管们可以说，“哇，这车看起来太酷了”，反正又不会出什么问题。最坏能怎样？大不了把漆撕掉嘛。（00:25:15）但问题是，如果有10个团队都在给车子加水钻，最终引擎盖会变得太重，根本抬不起来了。这正是大多数产品团队会遇到的困境。当越来越多的团队添加这些小功能、进行小改进、增添新特性（这些特性或许能获得一些用户，但无法提升核心价值，也不会影响商业引擎的运转）时，团队越多，引擎盖就越重，产品越复杂。（00:25:50）这些零零碎碎的功能彼此高度依赖，最终产品变成了一个松散连接的功能集合，而非单一的引导式体验。这意味着什么？这意味着内部协作变得极其困难。每次想开发新功能时，都得协调10个产品团队的依赖关系，于是公司开始增设项目管理层级。他们会说：“我们开会太多了。得重组项目管理部门，因为重组能解决一切问题。我们要确保层级清晰、团队协作、做好依赖管理。” 但随着层级增多，高影响力工作的难度也随之增加。（00:26:33）引擎盖越重，团队就越深陷低影响力工作的泥潭。低影响力工作滋生低影响力工作。你做越多低影响力工作，就越难开展高影响力工作，也就越容易陷入低影响力工作循环，如此反复，直到下一轮裁员。这确实是个严重的问题。（00:27:01）我在几乎所有合作过的公司都经历过这种情况。有趣的是，打破这个循环往往需要产品团队勇于审视自身工作，明确对业务的核心价值，说：“我们不能再甘当低影响力团队了。我们要主动寻找高影响力工作，全力交付，即便这意味着要跨团队协作。”
许多其他团队。即便这意味着高管团队突然对我们正在做的工作产生了极大的兴趣，我们也会将此视为我们所做工作意义重大的信号，而非阻碍我们完成工作的障碍。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: As you just kind of alluded to, there's a big implication here of even if you are told to build a thing that the execs are really excited about, that is low impact in your opinion, that's no excuse. You're still going to get fired eventually, even though they're telling you to build it. It sucks, but that's how it goes.
turns.zh: 正如你刚刚暗示的，这里有一个重要的隐含意思：即便被要求开发一款高管们极为兴奋的产品，但如果你认为其影响力微乎其微，那也绝不是借口。即便公司要求你去开发这款产品，最终你还是会被解雇。这确实很糟糕，但现实就是如此。

turns.speaker: Matt LeMay
turns.en: It's funny, I worked with MailChimp for three years leading up to their acquisition by Intuit, when they were on this really interesting journey of going from a single product company to a platform company, which is a journey that a lot of companies are on. Where they've found success in one part of the market and they say, "You know what? We recognize that there's a value add in working more horizontally and giving people a suite of tools they can use. We want to build these tools and really make sure that we are meeting the needs of our small and medium business customers." (00:28:34): So I was brought on shortly after they did a reorg. They went into a domains model. They had different teams that were supposed to be experts on different parts of this marketing platform that were building in new features and their VP product, Natalia Williams, who then became their CPO, she said, "This is great that we're doing this, but I'm worried that we're going to lose sight of the commercial fundamentals. We have these teams building this really cool stuff and we've been so clear that we're excited about the teams that are working on initiative, that are building these new things, that are building out this platform, but let's make sure we stay focused on making sure that the entire platform grows in a healthy and sustainable way. And that as we are adding in these new features and functionalities, we're not making this so crowded and complicated that it's harder for people to get value out of it." (00:29:31): So she set a very clear goal for the product team. She wanted a specific change in the rate of users who successfully send their first email. She was like, "As we build these new things, email is still where people are coming in. We want to make sure that they can do this successfully." And she set a really ambitious goal for the entire product organization. And she put it forth to the product teams and a lot of product teams were understandably hesitant to take this on, for a number of reasons. They said, "If we mess this up, that's the entire commercial heart of the business. That's really risky." (00:30:12): Other ones said, "That's great, but we're building out these new parts of the platform that are really important. We don't want to risk slowing those things down." There was one product manager I worked with who really understood how important this was. She had worked on enough different parts of the app at that point. She had been on a growth team, so she really had that kind of user-centric, how do we hit the metrics we need to hit mindset? And she came to me and she was like, "I want to make sure we do this because I'm worried about what'll happen if we don't do this, right? I don't want to be on the product team that failed to deliver what matters most to the business." (00:30:53): So she went and worked with some user researchers and found where people were getting stuck. She did this amazing study finding where people were getting stuck before they sent that first email and she gathered together a group of product managers. I'll never forget this. I was on site in Atlanta and she gathered together a group of product managers and she was like, "Look, these are the things we need to fix if we're going to hit this, but if we fix these things, I think we can do it. I think we can get there." And there was a moment of silence where again, for totally understandable reasons, people were like, "Okay, this is great. I see it, but I'm kind of afraid that if we do this," and this product manager, I will never forget that. (00:31:34): She looks around the room and she says, "You know what? I'm going to haunt all of you in your dreams if you do not take this on. This is the most important thing for the business." And everyone laughed. It was a strong comment, but it was a strong comment made in really good faith that in its own way, I think acknowledged the fear that people had about taking this on. She was like, "Look, this is really important and if we work together, if we care less about the constraints and parameters and borders of our domains and care more about how we work together to deliver the thing that our leader has told us is the most important thing for the business, we can get this done." (00:32:15): And they did get it done, and they got it done through subtracting. They streamlined the experience. They took out steps that people were getting stuck on. They made things easier. They did the kinds of things that are rarely celebrated in the way that traditional feature launches were celebrated, but because they had this clear, impactful, specific sense of what success looks like, they were able to take on that work themselves and it made the product better, made the business better, and it was just a great moment of working with a great team.
turns.zh:
挺有意思的，我在Intuit收购MailChimp之前，曾为该公司工作了三年。当时他们正经历一个非常有趣的转型，从单一产品公司向平台型公司转型，这也是许多公司正在经历的历程。他们在某个细分市场取得成功后，会意识到横向扩展并为用户提供一套工具能创造更大价值，于是决定打造这些工具，真正满足中小型企业客户的需求。（00:28:34）：我在他们重组后不久加入。当时他们转向了领域模型，各个团队专注于营销平台不同模块的开发。产品副总裁Natalia Williams（后来成为首席产品官）曾表示：“这样做固然很好，但我担心我们会忽视商业基础。我们团队在创新功能、构建平台方面做得很棒，但必须确保整个平台能健康、可持续地发展。在添加新功能时，别让产品变得过于复杂，让用户难以获得价值。”（00:29:31）：她为产品团队设定了一个明确目标——提升首次发送邮件成功率。她强调：“在开发新功能时，邮件功能仍是用户入口，我们必须确保其正常运作。”这个目标极具挑战性，产品团队普遍心存顾虑。有人担心：“若搞砸了，整个商业核心业务都完了。风险太大了。”也有人表示：“这想法很棒，但我们正全力开发关键模块，暂停这些功能会拖后腿。”但一位深知此事重要性的产品经理曾与我合作。她在产品团队工作多年后，深谙以用户为中心、达成关键指标的思维。她找到我，说：“我必须参与这个项目，因为不达成目标对业务影响太大了。我不想成为未能完成核心任务的产品团队成员。”（00:30:12）：她与用户研究团队合作，分析用户在首次发送邮件前的卡点问题。她组织产品经理们开会，我永远难忘那一幕。我在亚特兰大现场见证了她召集团队：“这些问题必须解决，否则目标无法达成。但只要克服这些障碍，我们就能成功。” 会场陷入沉默，人们带着完全可以理解的担忧说：“好主意，但真担心会出问题。” 那位产品经理的敬业精神令我难忘。（00:31:34）：
她环顾房间，说道："你们知道吗？如果你们不接手这项任务，我就会在你们的梦里缠着你们。这对公司来说是最重要的事。"众人听了都笑了。这番言辞虽然强硬，但确是出于真心。我认为她这样做恰恰认可了人们对承担这项任务的恐惧。她说："听着，这件事至关重要。如果我们齐心协力，不再纠结于各自领域的条条框框，而是专注于如何共同完成领导交付的核心任务，我们一定能成功。"（00:32:15）最终，他们确实做到了。他们通过精简流程完成了任务。他们移除了那些让用户卡壳的步骤，让操作更便捷。他们所做的一切，并非传统意义上的"功能发布"所能获赞，但正因为他们对成功有着清晰、务实且具体的定义，才得以自主推进项目，最终让产品更出色，让业务更高效。这确实是与优秀团队共事的辉煌时刻。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That was an awesome example. I love just how much of a hero's journey this example is. Along those lines, it's interesting how much courage it takes to do this. Because to your point, the easy thing is just, "Okay, everyone's just telling us to do this thing. We're going to build this feature. Great, easy. I don't have to put myself out there." And what you're pointing out there is it's up to you to recognize what you're doing is not high impact and to have courage to push back and suggest something else.
turns.zh: 那个例子真是太棒了。我特别喜欢这个例子所展现的英雄之旅的内涵。说到这里，要做到这件事需要多大的勇气啊？因为正如你所说，最简单的做法就是：“好吧，大家都让我们做这个功能。那就建吧，很简单。我没必要主动站出来。”而你所强调的是，关键在于你要意识到自己正在做的事情缺乏高价值，然后要有勇气反驳并提出新的建议。

turns.speaker: Matt LeMay
turns.en: The funny thing is, it's courage, but it's also a kind of radical acceptance of reality. There's a very kind of emotional philosophical dimension to this conversation because I think it is in human nature to not want to be accountable for things outside of our control. Impact is not something we can just check off a list. If we're really working towards business impact, that means that there are things that might happen in the market that are going to affect us, right? Our competitors might launch something, there might be a pandemic or a war or something we didn't expect. We're reliant upon customers to change their behavior, to convert or to upgrade or to do whatever it is we hope they will do. (00:33:58): I use the word hope because again, we can do our best to influence that behavior, but we can't just check a box. And I think there is this very understandable human fear of being accountable for things that are beyond our control. I get that so hard, but what I think the last couple of years have shown us is that we are accountable for things outside of our control. The success of the businesses we work for is ultimately beyond our immediate control. (00:34:26): And you can follow all the best practices and have the highest velocity and do everything quote-unquote "right", but if your company goes out of business, they're not going to say, "Yeah, we're going out of business, but we're going to keep writing your paycheck for two years because all of your OKRs were a 0.6 or a 0.7." That's not how it works. The reality is that things outside of our control affect us, and I think that if we can internalize that, there's a real freedom in it. The thing that surprised me most when I was researching this book is that the commercially minded PMs I interviewed were also the happiest, which I did not expect at all. (00:35:06): As you said, I come from a music background. I was expecting the business people to be really stressed out, and like, "I have to show up at work 92 hours a day to crush it and make sure that we hit the metrics and crush the numbers." But they were just like, "Yeah, I work for a business and I do the best I can, and then I go home. When I'm at work, my job is to help the business succeed. And I do that by understanding our business model, by trying to do work that contributes to what the business wants. In order to do that, if my goals are really impact level goals, I have to learn about our customers. I have to do discovery, I have to do all these things that we're supposed to do, not because they're abstract best practices, but because that's how you build a successful product." (00:35:49): And then at the end of the day, I'm not fighting my company to do product the right way, and if they can't do it the right way, I'm willing to die on this hill. It's like, " I work for a company. I don't get to make every decision. There are things outside of my control. I'll do the best I can, and I get to free up a little bit of energy to live the rest of my life."
turns.zh: 很有趣的是，这既需要勇气，也是一种对现实的彻底接纳。这场对话带有深刻的情感哲学内涵，因为我认为人类天生不愿为超出自身控制范围的事物负责。影响力不是我们能简单勾选完成的任务。如果我们真心致力于实现商业影响力，就意味着市场中可能出现的变数会对我们产生影响——比如竞争对手推出新产品、疫情爆发、战争或其他意外情况。我们依赖客户改变行为、完成转化或升级等目标。（00:33:58）我之所以用“希望”这个词，是因为我们确实能尽力影响客户行为，但无法简单对照清单打勾。我深知人们对超出控制范围的事物产生恐惧的心理，这是完全可以理解的。但过去几年的经历告诉我们，面对超出控制范围的局面，我们必须承担责任。我们所服务企业的成功最终超出我们直接掌控的范围。（00:34:26）你可以遵循所有最佳实践，保持最高的执行效率，尽一切努力做到“正确”，但如果公司倒闭了，他们不会说：“是的，我们要倒闭了，但会继续给你发两年工资，因为你的OKR得分是0.6或0.7。”现实就是，超出我们控制范围的因素会影响我们。我认为，如果我们能真正接受这一点，就能获得真正的自由。在研究这本书时，最令我惊讶的是，接受采访的商业导向型产品经理反而是最快乐的，这完全出乎我的意料。（00:35:06）正如你所说，我来自音乐行业。我原以为商业人士会压力巨大，每天工作92小时只为达成业绩指标。但他们却说：“是的，我为公司工作尽最大努力，然后回家。工作时我的职责是助力公司成功。为此，如果我的目标是影响力级别的，我就必须了解客户，进行探索，完成所有该做的事——这并非抽象的best practice，而是打造成功产品的关键。”（00:35:49）最终，我不会与公司对抗以正确的方式做产品。若他们无法正确执行，我愿意为此抗争到底。就像：“我为公司工作，不能掌控一切。有些事超出我的控制范围。我会尽最大努力，然后腾出精力享受余生。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To make this even less scary, hopefully, I'm curious what your answer is going to be here. Do you find that people who take this leap and push back and try to change the way their teams are thinking and what they take on, do you find that even if they fail, even if they impact wasn't there and the project fails, they're seen more favorably and their career ends up doing better and they end up doing better even if the project fails?
turns.zh: 为了让这件事不那么可怕，希望能听听你的看法。你是否发现，那些勇于突破、推动团队思维转变、承担新任务的人，即便失败了，即便项目未能达成影响力，人们对他们的评价也会更高，他们的职业生涯也会因此受益，即便项目失败了？

turns.speaker: Matt LeMay
turns.en: I hope so. I'm always super, again, it's outside of my control. I can't say, if you do these things, then you will be looked upon favorably by the people who manage you because I don't know those people, and maybe they're not going to react well. Maybe they're not actually... People are not always rational, and these things don't always play out the way you hope they will. What I will say is there's a story in the book, in Impact-First Product Teams about somebody who worked for a dating app, and they were given a project to work on, which had a very specific ambitious revenue goal. And at a certain point, it became clear that they were probably not going to be able to hit this because of other things they needed to do. (00:37:15): So they went to the finance team and said, "Hey, we have to adjust this down." And the finance team said, "Yeah, of course you do. That makes sense. Let's adjust it down together." Would that conversation have played out the same way if they had not taken that step of saying proactively, " Based on what is happening in the broader world in the market, our product, we no longer believe we are on track to hit this, but we want to adjust so that the company at large can make better predictions and resource things accordingly"? (00:37:42): I don't know. But I think again, if you are embracing that mindset that there are things outside of your control and your job is to do what you can from where you sit to contribute to the success of the business, I think you're certainly doing so much more by telling the business honestly what you think is possible and what's going to happen, as opposed to stepping back from it and saying like, "Oh, well, if we talk about it, we're going to get in trouble and nobody's going to believe us." And just that simple withholding of information does its own kind of harm. So I can't guarantee any kind of outcomes. I can't say, "Yes, this will be received with generosity and grace," in all cases, but I think it's the right thing to do.
turns.zh: 希望如此吧。我总是特别坦诚，这其实超出了我的控制范围。我不能保证，如果你做了这些事，就一定能得到上级赏识，因为我不了解那些人，说不定他们反应不佳。人性本就不总是理性的，事情的发展也未必如你所愿。不过我可以说，在《以影响力为先的产品团队》一书中有个案例，讲的是某家交友应用的员工接到一个项目，设定了极高的营收目标。但后来发现，由于其他优先事项的存在，这个目标根本无法达成。（00:37:15）于是他们去找财务团队说：“嘿，我们得把目标下调了。”财务团队回应：“嗯，当然应该这么做，合情合理。一起调整吧。”但如果他们不主动告知：“根据市场大环境和产品现状，我们认为达成这个目标已无望，但希望调整后能让公司更准确地预测并合理分配资源”，结果会不会有所不同？（00:37:42）我不确定。但我认为，如果你秉持“有些事超出我的控制范围，我能做的就是尽力为公司的成功贡献力量”的心态，坦诚地向公司说明你的判断，远比退缩不言要高明得多。退缩只会让人怀疑你的动机。信息的刻意隐瞒本身就是一种伤害。所以我无法保证具体结果，也不能保证所有人都心怀感激，但我认为这才是正确的做法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: My sense is either you will be respected more highly because you are kind of solving problems for people, like higher ups that you're seeing, things that they should be seeing, and you're right, and they're like, "Oh, wow, Matt's amazing. He saw all this stuff and changed." Or you realize this is not the company for me. They don't value this. They just want me to ship this widget and that's all they want from me. I could do more somewhere else.
turns.zh: 我的感觉是，要么你会赢得更多尊重，因为你为上级解决了问题，比如他们本该注意到却忽视的问题，而你能看清全局并做出改变，他们会说：“哇，马特太棒了。他发现了这些问题，推动了改进。”要么你会意识到这家公司不适合你。他们不重视这些创新，只想让你按部就班完成任务。我可以在其他地方发挥更大价值。

turns.speaker: Matt LeMay
turns.en: Well, I think you touched on something really important there, which is that when you understand the business model, you understand the real world ethics and priorities of the company you work for, right? If you understand what the company's optimizing for, what they really care about, what trade-offs and sacrifices they're willing to make in order to achieve those goals, that tells you a lot more than the mission statement. Which usually sounds great, but if you follow the money, if you follow the decision-making, sometimes it paints a different picture. (00:39:28): And I think the more you can understand how the business model works, what that value exchange is, what value is being delivered, what value is being extracted, that I think puts you in a better position to decide, if I were to help the company achieve success, do I feel good about that? Do I feel like this is a company that if it achieves its goals has made the world a better place or not? And the more you understand the business model, the better equipped you are to make those decisions with all the information available to you, I think.
turns.zh: 嗯，我觉得你刚才提到了一个非常重要的问题，那就是当你理解了商业模式，你就能理解所在公司的真实商业伦理和优先事项，对吧？如果你能理解公司的优化目标、真正关心的重点，以及为了实现这些目标愿意做出的权衡和牺牲，这比单纯看使命宣言要深刻得多。使命宣言通常听起来很美好，但如果你追根溯源，关注决策过程，有时会发现截然不同的现实。（00:39:28）我认为，当你越能理解商业模式如何运作、价值交换是什么、传递了什么价值、提取了什么价值时，你就越能更好地做出判断：如果我要帮助公司取得成功，我会对此感到心安吗？我会觉得这家公司如果达成目标就能让世界变得更美好吗？当你越了解商业模式，就越能在掌握所有信息的基础上做出这些决定，我觉得这很重要。

You can throw 100-page strategy document at it and ask it for insights, or you can dump all your user research and ask it to find patterns. With Claude 4 and the new integrations, including Claude 4 Opus, the world's best coding model, you get voice conversations, advanced research capabilities, direct Google Workspace integration, and now MCP connections to your custom tools and data sources. That's claude.ai/lenny. (00:41:24): Okay, so let's shift to talking about how to actually, what to do. This concept of actions you can take regardless of how your company operates.
